title: The Day of Pardon (2000)
hook: in St Peter's, the pope publicly asks forgiveness for sins committed by Catholics through history

segments.voice: Yesterday, World Youth Day: a wooden cross on the move, and the pilgrimage to a night in a field. Your line was the young gather. Who did you listen to all the way through? Day nine hundred twenty-eight.

On a Sunday in Lent, in St Peter's Basilica, a crucifix stands near an old pope. One after another, cardinals and bishops step forward. Each names a kind of wrong. Not wrongs done to the Church. Wrongs done by its own members. After each one there's silence, and then the pope speaks a prayer asking pardon, and the people answer. Before it ends, the pope goes to the crucifix and kisses it. He was John Paul the Second, frail by then. The Church remembers it as the Day of Pardon. A very old institution, under its own famous dome, saying out loud: we did this.
screen: `A CRUCIFIX IN ST PETER'S.` → `WRONGS DONE BY ITS OWN MEMBERS.` → `WE DID THIS.`

segments.voice: The prayers came in a set order. First, what was named. The prayers asked forgiveness for sins committed in the service of truth, for divisions among Christians, for sins against the people of Israel, for wrongs against love, peace and the dignity of peoples and cultures, against women, against the poor and the unborn. They were broad on purpose. Some listeners wanted more names and details; some thought it went too far. Both reactions were real. Second, who was asking. The Church teaches that the Church itself is holy, and also that its members sin. So the prayers were spoken for the sins of her sons and daughters, the members, past and present. Theologians had spent time on exactly that distinction and wrote a document about it, called Memory and Reconciliation. Third, the scripture underneath. The first letter of John says it plainly, in the Douay-Rheims: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us." A Church that says that to each person in confession was saying it about itself. Fourth, the other half. In his homily that day the pope paired two things: we forgive, and we ask forgiveness. Catholics have an old phrase for owning a wrong, from the Confiteor, one of the prayers that can open Mass: through my fault. On that day it was said by a whole Church, about its own history. What it did not do was settle everything. An apology spoken in Rome is a beginning. What comes after it is the hard part, and some of that story comes tomorrow.
screen: `SINS NAMED, ONE BY ONE.` · `A HOLY CHURCH, MEMBERS WHO SIN.` · `IF WE SAY WE HAVE NO SIN.` · `WE FORGIVE, AND WE ASK FORGIVENESS.` · then, large: `THE TRUTH IS NOT IN US.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask forgiveness for your part. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something that went wrong between you and someone else, where the blame is shared. Don't add up their part. Just find your own piece of it, small or large, and name it plainly to yourself, the way those bishops did: one sentence, no excuses. If you pray, you can bring it to God, perhaps with the old words, through my fault. If you don't, just hold it honestly, without punishing yourself. The bell holds the time.
Mea culpa. Through my fault, the old phrase from the Confiteor that the whole Church said about its own history on the Day of Pardon.
Your line: we ask forgiveness. Today, if there's someone owed an apology for your part, say it in one sentence, with no but at the end. Day nine hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Catholics confess their own sins in the sacrament of penance and say the Confiteor, with its words through my fault, at the start of Mass; the Day of Pardon brought that language to the Church's own history.
